summary: This talk dissects common pitfalls and hard truths about pitching video games, distilling practical guidance into 30 concise observations. The speaker emphasizes pitches should answer two core questions (is the game worth making, and can the team execute it) and warns against overloading a pitch with lore, standard systems, or superficial polish. Key lessons include distinguishing a compelling hook from supporting pillars, clearly describing moment-to-moment gameplay, avoiding heavy backstories and demos that don’t prove the concept, and resisting the temptation to chase the latest tech or a flashy monetization plan. The talk also covers prototyping focus, art direction, dialogue quality, licensing risks, scope realism, and the interpersonal dynamics of working with publishers. The speaker closes with practical tips on preparation, presentation tools, and handling questions, reinforced by examples and counterexamples from industry practice.
title: 30 Things I Hate About Your Game Pitch
topics: Two core pitch questions: is the game worth making? can the team execute it?
Avoid heavy backstory in pitches; lore dump distracts from core concept
How to reference Star Wars-like quick setup as an example rather than lengthy exposition
Don’t dump standard or non-core features unless they’re central to the concept
Don’t invite the audience to design the game during the pitch; present your vision
Pillars are not hooks; emphasize a unique selling proposition (hook) early
Describe moment-to-moment gameplay, not just setting or visuals
Realism as justification: avoid excuses for design decisions unless you’re doing hardcore simulation
Frame stories (game shows) are often unnecessary; remove unless there is a strong reason
Be wary of parody as a selling point; it can signal underlying issues with the concept
Explicitly acknowledge technical risks and explain mitigation plans
Proof of concept: prototype should showcase a unique or hard-to-build element, not trivial mechanics
Art direction: one stellar image can sell the look better than many mediocre visuals; placeholders help distinguish final intent
Polished visuals too early can be a red flag if mechanics are incomplete
Dialogue quality matters; showcase strong writing rather than placeholder dialogue
Tech hype (VR/AR, etc.) should fit the game concept; avoid retrofitting to chase trends
IP licensing risk: avoid relying on IP you do not own; licensing should be settled beforehand
Monetization details belong later; share basic monetization direction but not granular pricing before development
Scope and feasibility: know hours, levels, dialogue, and cost; a solid plan supports feasibility
Team and hiring roadmap: demonstrate leads and hiring plan to execute the project
Professionalism and collaboration: pitch performance reflects how you’d function under stress
Traction metrics and track record: note any past shipped titles or relevant successes to bolster feasibility
Trailer vs prototype: use trailers judiciously; strong prototype and gameplay proof are often more persuasive
Preparation and targeting: research publishers/investors to tailor the pitch to their interests
